newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-French stocks plunge on poll jitters.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French stocks plunge on poll jitters.

text.p: French shares plunged and the franc slipped on Monday after the combined left defied most expectations to outpoll the ruling centre-right coalition in the first round of France's parliamentary election.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index opened down 106.03 points or 3.84 percent at 2,656.87 and at 0915 GMT it was still down almost three percent.

The French franc extended overnight losses against the mark but quickly stabilised and traders said they did not expect a rout. The franc fell as low as 3.3755 per mark overnight from 3.3714 before the first election results were released. It was trading at 3.3757 at 0915 GMT.

"Clearly, I think certain institutions don't want (the mark) to climb too quickly," one trader said. "From my point of view the levels (of the mark) are not that expensive and I think it will climb again."

Elsewhere on the currency front the dollar picked up from overnight lows against the mark and steadied in morning Europe. Dollar/yen was also steady at firmer levels from Friday, just shy of 116 yen. Dealers said trade was thin because of market holidays in both Britain and the U.S.
Paris was the main centre of attention . Investors, betting on a good showing by France's conservative RPR-UDF coalition, had driven the CAC-40 up 0.78 percent to close at 2,762.90 points on Friday.

But projections broadcast after voting ended at 1800 GMT on Sunday gave the opposition Socialists, Communists, extreme-left and other left candidates between 40.6 and 41.6 percent of the vote, with the ruling RPR-UDF and other moderate-right candidates scoring between 36.1 and 37.1 percent.

"The stock market, putting its trust in opinion polls showing the right would win, had treated the election as a non-event. We are going to pay for it because the market had not taken the political risk fully into account," a dealer said.

"We are faced with the worst possible scenario. Is the right going to return the votes in their favour in the second round? If the left wins, what is going to happen to the Maastricht Treaty? And what about issues such as (defence electronics firm and privatisation candidate) Thomson," another dealer said.

A dealer in Madrid was more sanguine, commenting: "The defeat of the centre-right coalition will have a negative effect on markets but it won't be anything special because what is really important is the second round."

Meanwhile, German shares, which started a shade weaker, picked up and were nearly one percent stronger by mid-morning, helped by the stabilising dollar and Friday's strong performance on Wall Street, where the Dow closed up 1.21 percent.
And in Brussels the blue chip Bel-20 Index surged to a new life high at the start of trade as a wave of what dealers described as merger mania continued to sweep the bourse.
Bank Kredietbank was the leading gainer, up 1.58 percent, on news that parent Almanij is to acquire Gevaert assets, and on continued speculation about talks with Dutch Rabobank.
STOCK PRICES AT 0915 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE 100 was closed for a market holiday. On Friday it closed up 10.0 points, or 0.21 percent, at 4,661.8.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 80 points or 2.88 percent at 2,683.
FRANKFURT - The DAX index was up 29 points at 3,631.
CURRENCIES AT 0915 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.6860 marks and 115.93 yen compared with 1.6910 marks and 115.49 yen in late European trade on Friday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold opened opened steady with a soft undertone at $342.90 in a very slack market due to the U.S. and UK holiday. Silver was one cent weaker at 474 cents.
